hero.title: How INFORM Tanzania measures risk
hero.lead: INFORM Tanzania applies the INFORM methodology of the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre to every council in the country. This page documents the model end to end, recomputes a real council in your browser, and states its limitations plainly.

overview.title: An open, reproducible index of disaster risk for every council
overview.lead: What INFORM is, what this Tanzanian implementation adds, and who it is built for.
overview.p1: INFORM (the Index for Risk Management) is a global, open-source assessment of the risk of humanitarian crises and disasters. It is a collaboration of the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) and the European Commission, with the Joint Research Centre (JRC) as scientific lead, and it is used by governments, UN agencies and donors to decide where to invest in preparedness and prevention.
overview.p2: INFORM treats risk as the meeting point of three dimensions: the hazards people are exposed to, how vulnerable they are, and how little capacity exists to cope. The dimensions are combined with a geometric mean, so a place is at high risk only where all three are present. A severe hazard in a well-prepared, resilient area is not scored as a disaster.
overview.p3: INFORM Tanzania brings that method down to where decisions are made. Its Core rebuilds the INFORM Tanzania country workbook (INFORM Sub-national SADC 2024) in code and reproduces it exactly: every Core score is the workbook’s own value, except the values the integrity recheck withholds from the live model until they are corrected (see Limitations), presented for the {{councils}} councils and {{regions}} regions of the 2022 Population and Housing Census through the workbook’s {{sources}} units. Tanzanian data enter in two ways: institutions update the workbook’s own indicators through the Data portal, and every other improvement (council hazard indices, survey measures on other definitions, expert assessments) belongs to a separate Advancement layer that is documented and shown apart from the Core, never mixed into it.

pipeline.title: From a raw measurement to a risk score in eight steps
pipeline.lead: Steps 1–4 standardise each raw value onto a common 0–10 scale; steps 5–8 aggregate it up the hierarchy. The formulas are those of the Tanzania INFORM workbook, cell for cell.
pipeline.intro: Standardisation follows the workbook’s processing sheets; aggregation follows the INFORM SADC 2024 sheet (cells Z, AK, AU and AV). Each stage is locked by a golden test against the workbook’s cached values. Because the minimum and maximum of every indicator are frozen, a value standardises identically whether the model runs on 170 units, 195 councils or any other resolution.
pipeline.applies: Applies to {{n}} of the {{total}} indicators in use.
pipeline.appliesMinmax: {{custom}} indicators use a fixed reference pair and {{range}} the frozen workbook data range; {{dec}} are inverted (Decrease risk).

where.denominator: where d is the denominator named in the specification (e.g. population).
where.quartiles: where L and U are Tukey’s fences: Q₁ and Q₃ are the lower and upper quartiles across units, and IQR = Q₃ − Q₁.
where.minmax: where min and max are the indicator’s frozen reference values, identical at every resolution.
where.weights: where the sums run over the indicators of the group that have data; wᵢ = 1 in standard INFORM.
where.components: where the sum runs over the m indicator groups of the category that have data.

1.title: Denominator
1.body: Counts are turned into rates where the specification requires it (for example, health facilities per inhabitant), so large and small units are compared fairly.
1.formula: x equals the raw value divided by the denominator d

2.title: Outlier cap (Tukey fences)
2.body: Where flagged, a value is clamped to the Tukey fences so that a single extreme unit cannot stretch the scale for everyone else.
2.formula: x prime equals the minimum of the maximum of x and Q1 minus 1.5 times IQR, and Q3 plus 1.5 times IQR

3.title: Transform
3.body: Heavily skewed indicators (event counts, exposure) are log-transformed; the 0.001 offset keeps a real zero finite.
3.formula: x double prime equals the natural logarithm of 0.001 plus x prime

4.title: Min–max to 0–10
4.body: The value is placed between the indicator’s frozen minimum and maximum, inverted where more means less risk (“Decrease risk”, e.g. physicians per capita), clamped to 0–10 and rounded to one decimal.
4.formula: s star equals 10 times x minus min over max minus min; for decrease-risk indicators s star becomes 10 minus s star; s equals s star clamped to 0 to 10 and rounded to one decimal

5.title: Indicator group = average
5.body: The standardised indicators of a group are averaged. Missing values are skipped, never treated as zero. In standard INFORM every weight is 1; weights matter only in the advanced multi-source baskets.
5.formula: g equals the sum of w i times s i over the sum of w i, over indicators with data

6.title: Category = average
6.body: Each category is the arithmetic mean of its indicator groups, again skipping groups without data.
6.formula: c equals the mean of the m indicator groups

7.title: Dimension = scaled geometric mean
7.body: Categories are mapped onto INFORM’s 1–10 “lack-of” scale, combined with a geometric mean and mapped back to 0–10. The result is never below the arithmetic mean, so a severe category is not diluted by a mild one. Rounded to one decimal.
7.formula: y k equals 10 minus c k, over 10, times 9, plus 1; D equals 10 minus the geometric mean of the y k, divided by 9, times 10, rounded to one decimal; the geometric mean of n values is the n-th root of their product

8.title: Risk = cube root of the product
8.body: INFORM Risk is the geometric mean of the three dimensions: risk is high only where hazard, vulnerability and lack of coping capacity coincide. Rounded to one decimal.
8.formula: Risk equals the cube root of H times V times LCC, rounded to one decimal

geometric.title: Why a geometric mean?
geometric.lead: The choice of aggregation encodes what risk means. INFORM uses two geometric means, with opposite emphases.
geometric.p1: An arithmetic mean lets a high score in one dimension compensate for a low score in another. Risk does not work that way: a strong earthquake in an empty desert is not a disaster, and a poor community with no hazard is not at risk of one. INFORM therefore multiplies the three dimensions (a geometric mean), so a very low value in any one of them pulls risk down.
geometric.p2: Inside a dimension INFORM does the opposite. The geometric mean is taken on the inverted (10 − c) scale, so the dimension is never lower than the arithmetic mean of its categories: a council facing a severe natural hazard keeps a high Hazard & Exposure score even if human-made hazards are negligible.
geometric.riskNote: When all three dimensions are equal, both means agree. When one dimension approaches zero, the geometric mean collapses towards zero while the arithmetic mean still reports moderate risk.
geometric.dimHint: Two categories of the Hazard & Exposure dimension.
geometric.dimNote: The scaled geometric mean always sits at or above the arithmetic mean: one severe category keeps the whole dimension high.

classification.title: Five classes, with separate thresholds for each dimension
classification.lead: Scores are classified with the cut-points in the Tanzania workbook’s Thresholds sheet. Each cut-point is an exclusive upper bound: a risk score of exactly {{t1}} is Low, not Very low.
classification.ruleLabel: class is Very low if x is below t1, Low if x is at least t1 and below t2, Medium if x is at least t2 and below t3, High if x is at least t3 and below t4, and Very high if x is at least t4
classification.ruleCaption: Workbook rule. t₁ … t₄ are the four thresholds of the scale; a score equal to a threshold belongs to the class above.
classification.visualTitle: The same 0–10 axis, cut differently for each scale
classification.visualLead: Hazard, vulnerability and lack of coping capacity are distributed differently across Tanzania, so each carries its own cut-points.
classification.tableCaption: Class boundaries by scale (score range, one decimal)
classification.own: Every map, badge, gauge and table in this application classifies a dimension with that dimension’s thresholds and INFORM Risk with the risk thresholds. Reusing the risk thresholds for a dimension (as the previous version of the tool did) misclassifies it, because the dimensions do not share a distribution.
classification.example: A score of {{value}} is {{hazardClass}} on the Hazard & Exposure scale but only {{riskClass}} on the INFORM Risk scale.

levels.title: Three administrative levels, one consistent model
levels.lead: The same engine runs at every level, and each level is built in the way INFORM prescribes, never by averaging scores that were already aggregated.

councils.title: Councils
councils.body: The {{n}} councils of the 2022 census. In the Core each council carries the scores of its INFORM source unit and its own census population; council-level data enter through the Data portal or the Advancement layer. Risk is computed live as ∛(H × V × LCC), so an approved update propagates at once.
councils.inherited: {{n}} new or split councils ({{examples}} …) inherit their parent district’s data until council-specific data exist. They are flagged wherever they appear, never fabricated.

regions.title: Regions
regions.body: The {{n}} regions are built from their councils the INFORM way: indicator means → category means → scaled geometric mean → cube root. A region’s risk is never a mean of council risk scores.

national.title: National (aggregate)
national.body: The national value, {{value}}, is the INFORM aggregate of all councils: indicator means, category means, scaled geometric mean and cube root, exactly as for regions. The Tanzania workbook publishes no national score, and the INFORM Global country score uses other indicators and is not comparable.

missing.title: Missing data is not zero
missing.body: A blank indicator is stored as “no data” (null) and excluded from every average, so it can neither raise nor lower a score. A 0 is different: it is included as a real low value. Two workbook indicators make it less than a measurement: coastal erosion scores 0 for every unit, coastal or not, because its reference range maps every value to 0, and livelihoods is 0 in most units (see Limitations).
missing.formula: the mean of 5, 5 and a missing value equals {{result}}, not 3.3

propagate.title: Updates propagate through every level
propagate.body: Sector data enters through the Data portal and is reviewed by PMO-DMD. Once approved, the council’s dimension is recomputed from its indicators, then its risk, then its region. A vulnerability or coping update on an INFORM source unit reaches every council that shares it.

shared.title: Shared source units
shared.body: Because survey data exist at the workbook’s resolution, {{n}} INFORM source units each supply vulnerability and coping values to more than one council. The Data portal says which councils an update will reach.

levels.liveNote: Council and regional scores on this site are recomputed from their indicators when the model loads. Approved updates currently applied: {{edits}}.
levels.boundaries: Boundary set: {{set}}. {{councils}} councils in {{regions}} regions and {{districts}} districts; the identifiers C001 to C{{councils}} are fixed by the council registry and change only through the boundary procedure (data-source/BOUNDARIES.md).

rule.title: How regions and the nation are built, and what other rules would give
rule.lead: A region, and the nation ({{national}}), takes the plain mean of its councils' indicator values; the categories, dimensions and risk then follow the INFORM rules. A workbook unit that backs two councils therefore counts twice. Two other rules are computed live as sensitivities; the Core keeps the plain mean until the SADC and INFORM partners adopt a weighting (decision D11).
rule.note: Shown as a sensitivity; no map uses it.

severity.title: Crisis severity: the official INFORM Severity Index method
severity.lead: INFORM Risk describes the structural likelihood of harm before a crisis. The INFORM Severity Index measures how severe an ongoing crisis is. INFORM Tanzania implements the JRC/ACAPS method for sub-national Tanzanian crises.
severity.p1: Severity is assessed on a 0–5 scale across three dimensions: the impact of the crisis, the conditions of the people affected, and the complexity of the crisis. The structure, weights and aggregation below follow the published concept and methodology.
severity.formulaLabel: Severity equals 0.7 times G of Impact with weight one third and Conditions with weight two thirds, plus 0.3 times Complexity
severity.formulaCaption: Impact and conditions combine through INFORM’s weighted geometric aggregation G, with weights 1/3 and 2/3; that result carries weight 0.7 and complexity 0.3.

steps.normalise: Each indicator is scaled to 0–5 between reference values (absolute counts on a log₁₀(1 + x) scale) and inverted where a higher value means lower severity.
steps.average: Indicators combine into components, and components into most categories, by arithmetic average (missing values skipped).
steps.geometric: Categories combine into dimensions with INFORM’s inverted, rescaled weighted geometric mean G, shown below.
steps.final: Severity = 0.7 × G(Impact 1/3, Conditions 2/3) + 0.3 × Complexity, calculated only when all three dimensions have data.

severity.gLabel: G of x with weights w equals 5 minus the exponential of the weighted mean of the natural logarithm of y i, minus 1, over 4, times 5, where y i equals 5 minus x i, times 4 over 5, plus 1
severity.gCaption: Invert, rescale to [1, 5], take the weighted geometric mean, rescale to [0, 5] and invert back. Fixed points: 0 → 0 and 5 → 5.
severity.categoriesLead: The category is the ROUNDUP of the one-decimal score (so 3.1 is category 4).
severity.reliability: A reliability rating from 1 to 5 (the average of source reliability, recency of the last update and the share of indicators with data) is shown alongside every result. It qualifies the score; it does not change it.
severity.citation: Poljanšek, K., Vernaccini, L. & Marin Ferrer, M. (2020). INFORM Severity Index: Concept and Methodology. European Commission JRC and ACAPS.
severity.calibration: Indicator reference ranges are calibration parameters for sub-national Tanzanian crises; they are listed in the calculator.

sources.title: Data sources register
sources.lead: Every indicator group, the dataset and method behind its Core value (all from the INFORM Sub-national SADC 2024 workbook), the resolution at which that data genuinely exist, and the Tanzanian institution responsible for keeping the group current. A regional value used for a council is labelled as regional.
sources.workbookLead: The full keying-in specification extracted from the Tanzania workbook: every raw indicator with its unit, processing, frozen reference, direction and resolution. Indicators with Use = Yes feed the model.
sources.captionGroups: Data sources for every indicator group
sources.note: Dataset and method descriptions are recorded in English as the workbook supplies them. The responsible institution is who is asked for updates; it is not the source of a value it did not supply. Downloads contain the rows currently shown.

limitations.title: Data notes and limitations
limitations.lead: What a reader must know about the data behind the scores: the workbook values withheld after validation, the groups the workbook leaves empty, the councils that inherit a neighbour’s data, where the data come from, and the Advancement layer shown beside the Core. The technical analyses (sensitivities, coherence, corrections) are reported in the assessment reports and the thesis.

global.title: Every Core indicator is a global dataset
global.now: All 53 scoring indicators of the workbook come from global sources (Global Data Lab, World Bank, WHO, JRC, FAO, GEM, ACLED and others). 15 carry one value for the whole country, 33 vary only between regions and 4 between districts, so most differences between councils in vulnerability and coping are differences between regions. Several are old: child mortality, underweight and immunisation cover 2006 to 2021. Since 11 October 2026 the two institutional groups also carry a council-level Tanzanian indicator each (DRM arrangements in place; disaster management committee functioning), recorded by the committees through the Data portal over the PMO-DMD lists.
global.next: Institutions replace the global proxies with Tanzanian data on the same definition through the Data portal: the 2022 census, the 2022 demographic and health survey and routine information systems.

empty.title: Six indicator groups are empty in the workbook; the Benchmark 2026 fills five
empty.now: The workbook leaves heatwave, lightning, zoonoses and pests, hazardous material, vehicle accidents and the economic vulnerable-groups indicator empty for every Tanzanian unit. The Benchmark 2026 activates five of them with Tanzanian data: heatwave days (ERA5-Land), lightning stroke density (WWLLN), recorded road crashes per 100 km² (police statistics, shared among councils by population so the big cities carry them), hazardous-material sites per 100 km² (OpenStreetMap, the 2022 census mapping and the NEMC certificates of July to September 2026) and female-headed households (2022 census). Zoonoses and pests stay empty and enter no score. Internal violence is withheld by programme decision (data note DN-12): the workbook keeps its ACLED counts, the live model shows no value. The density of health facilities can never score in the workbook (its range is 0 to 0).
empty.next: Fill zoonoses and pests from the One Health surveillance of the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Livestock and Fisheries; extend the NEMC certificate series month by month; report the degenerate indicators to the SADC and INFORM partners.

inherit.title: {{inherited}} councils inherit a neighbour’s unit
inherit.now: Councils created or split after the workbook’s boundaries (Kibiti, Ubungo and Kigamboni among them) carry the values of the unit they were carved from until council-specific data exist. They are flagged, never fabricated. With them, 25 workbook units each back two councils.
inherit.next: Council-level values entered by institutions take precedence for that council alone (finest level wins).

advanced.title: The Advancement layer is shown apart, with gaps
advanced.now: Since October 2026 the Advancement layer is computed from the filled sub-indicators (council climate and terrain indices from CHIRPS, ERA5-Land, MODIS, SMAP, SRTM and the USGS catalogue) and shown on every profile beside the Core. Thirteen of the 25 sub-indicators are unfilled or withheld; the indices measure intensity rather than exposed people; the weights are proposed and the reference ranges relative. The survey measures and expert grades that the site showed before October 2026 are not in it: they need a source, a method and a date before they can enter.
advanced.next: Fill the remaining baskets (TMA, basin boards, NEMC, GEM, LIS/OTD), convert intensity to exposed population on the census grid, calibrate the weights against recorded events, then decide the default view (decision D2).

queried.title: {{withheld}} values are withheld from the live model; {{replaced}} were replaced by approved values
queried.now: The indicator-by-indicator recheck of 10 October 2026 compared every workbook value with documented events, with the other indicators of the workbook and with each indicator's own definition. It found values that contradict them: Dar es Salaam's drought frequency, the semi-arid Lake zone's drought minimum, Kagera's earthquake exposure, Ukerewe's landslide exposure, Dodoma's electricity access, the displaced-people and food-security rows and the coastal-erosion rows. The live model withholds them, as INFORM treats data that fails validation: the group is missing for those units ({{withheld}} values, {{withheldUnits}} workbook units, {{withheldCouncils}} councils; a group with other indicators is recomputed from them), and every place that shows the value says so with the note. The workbook itself is kept exactly and proven by the tests; {{notes}} notes on {{noteGroups}} indicator groups reach {{councils}} councils. Of the {{withheldWorkbook}} workbook values the recheck quarantined, the Benchmark 2026 of 10 October 2026 replaced {{replaced}} council values with approved institutional values (coastal erosion, cyclone exposure, food security, displacement, Dodoma's electricity, Ukerewe's landslide); {{withheld}} remain withheld in {{withheldCouncils}} councils (agricultural drought for Dar es Salaam, not applicable to a city).
queried.next: The queries are raised with INFORM (JRC) and SADC for the next workbook release (docs/assessment/INFORM_TZ_Upstream_Queries_{{release}}.md); an institution replaces a withheld value through the Data portal with a citable source, which lifts the hold for that unit. The register is docs/assessment/INFORM_TZ_Indicator_Integrity_{{release}}.md, regenerated with every release.

limitations.closing: Each item above is tracked, and each can be improved through the Data portal or in code without changing the INFORM engine. As gaps close, scores will change as the picture becomes more complete, and every change remains traceable to a sourced indicator.
limitations.sourcesNote: Sources: INFORM Tanzania Methodology & Data-Integrity Manual (§8), Local Data Integration Plan (§2) and the Indicator Source Register.

summary.lead: How INFORM Tanzania measures risk, in seven short sections. Each opens to its full documentation page.

pipeline.title: From a raw measurement to a risk score

steps.1: Each raw value becomes a 0–10 score by the workbook’s specification for that indicator: denominator, outlier fence, logarithm, reference range and direction of effect.
steps.2: Indicators average into their indicator group, and groups into their category, over the members with data: a missing value never counts as zero.
steps.3: The two categories of a dimension combine by INFORM’s scaled geometric mean, rounded to one decimal: one severe category keeps the dimension high.
steps.4: Risk is the cube root of Hazard & Exposure × Vulnerability × Lack of Coping Capacity: high only where all three are present.

documentation.title: Full documentation
documentation.lead: The complete methodology, one page per section, for analysts and reviewers: the specification cell for cell, the live worked example, the crisis severity method, the sources register, the data notes and the references.

levels.councils: The {{n}} councils of the 2022 census carry the scores of their workbook unit ({{units}} units) and their own census population; approved council values apply to that council alone.
levels.regions: The {{n}} regions are built from their councils the INFORM way (indicator means, category means, scaled geometric mean, cube root), never by averaging risk scores.
levels.national: The national value, {{value}}, is the same aggregate over all councils. The workbook publishes no national score and INFORM Global is not comparable.
